after.name: Inflationary curvature power spectrum
after.description: Leading slow-roll scalar curvature-perturbation spectrum in natural units.
assumptions: Canonical minimally coupled single scalar in an approximately spatially flat background; leading slow roll, unit scalar sound speed and the usual adiabatic short-wavelength vacuum.
The displayed M_Pl is the REDUCED Planck mass (8πG)^(-1/2). PDG uses unreduced M_P = G^(-1/2); its equation (23.48) becomes this expression only after M_P² = 8π M_Pl².
Here epsilon denotes epsilon_H = -Hdot/H²; at the retained order epsilon_H ≈ epsilon_V. Evaluate the background at Hubble exit k = aH.

Identifying the late conserved curvature spectrum requires an adiabatic attractor and no subsequent entropy-to-curvature transfer. The curvature normalization is ill-defined in the exact epsilon = 0 limit.
variables: P_R: dimensionless scalar curvature power per logarithmic wavenumber
epsilon: Hubble slow-roll parameter at leading order
after.regime: Leading single-field slow-roll scalar spectrum, not a formula for arbitrary inflation or non-attractor evolution.
after.units: c = ħ = 1; H and M_Pl have mass dimension one; epsilon and P_R are dimensionless.
after.theoryRelationship: Observed scalar spectra constrain this conditional prediction; the expression alone does not establish a unique quantum origin.

sourceLocations.locator: Section 23.3.3 equation (23.48), PDF p. 9; convention conversion from p. 1 footnote 1 and epsilon definitions (23.11),(23.15) p. 4. Equation uses P_zeta, agreeing in power with P_R for the stated super-Hubble adiabatic limit.

after.name: Mukhanov–Sasaki equation
after.description: Mode equation for scalar cosmological perturbations in single-field inflation.
assumptions: Linear scalar perturbations of a canonical minimally coupled single-field spatially flat FLRW background; the equation itself does not require slow roll.
Primes in this equation denote derivatives with respect to conformal time, not field derivatives. k is comoving wavenumber.

z = a phidot/H and v = aQ, where Q is the gauge-invariant field perturbation on spatially flat slices. PDG uses R = -HQ/phidot; an overall curvature-sign convention does not change this mode equation.
Use a regular background interval with a well-defined z and z second derivative divided by z; field turning points require care. Noncanonical or multiple-field systems have modified equations.
variables: a: scale factor (called R in the source background notation)
after.regime: Exact linear mode equation for the stated canonical single-field spatially flat FLRW system; quantum predictions additionally require a state and mode normalization.
after.units: c = ħ = 1 with dimensionless a; k and inverse conformal time have mass dimension one, so k² and z second derivative/z have mass dimension two.
after.theoryRelationship: Dynamical equation underlying the inflationary scalar spectrum, not a measured spectrum by itself.

sourceLocations.locator: Section 23.3.3 equations (23.41)–(23.43), PDF p. 9; Q and curvature sign in (23.27)–(23.28), PDF pp. 6–7.

after.name: Scalar spectral index
after.plain: n_s-1 = d ln P_R/d ln k ~ -6 epsilon +2 eta
after.description: Leading slow-roll expression for the scalar spectral tilt.
assumptions: The logarithmic derivative defines the tilt; its final approximate equality is first-order canonical single-field potential slow roll.
Here epsilon means epsilon_V and eta means eta_V, not a Hubble-flow eta parameter. In reduced-mass notation epsilon_V = M_Pl²(Vprime/V)²/2 and eta_V = M_Pl²Vsecond/V.
Use the standard short-wavelength vacuum and an adiabatic attractor; evaluate parameters when the stated comoving pivot exits k = aH. Higher-order terms and subsequent transfer can modify the result.
after.regime: First-order canonical single-field slow roll; the definition remains meaningful when that approximation fails.
after.units: c = ħ = 1; index, slow-roll parameters and logarithmic derivative dimensionless.
after.theoryRelationship: Connects a restricted potential model to scale dependence, not a unique reconstruction of the potential.

sourceLocations.locator: Section 23.3.3 equation (23.51), PDF p. 10, with potential definitions (23.15), PDF p. 4; convert unreduced M_P² = 8π M_Pl².

after.name: Tensor-to-scalar ratio
after.description: Leading single-field slow-roll tensor-to-scalar ratio.
assumptions: P_T includes both tensor polarizations and numerator and denominator are evaluated at the same pivot.
The approximate equality assumes canonical minimally coupled single-field slow roll, scalar sound speed one, standard vacuum and no late entropy-to-curvature transfer.
Here epsilon can be epsilon_H or epsilon_V only to the retained leading slow-roll order; the distinction matters beyond that order.
variables: r: tensor-to-scalar power ratio at a stated pivot
after.regime: Leading-order single-field slow-roll relation; not a universal tensor/scalar identity beyond the defining ratio.
after.units: Both spectra, r and epsilon are dimensionless.
after.theoryRelationship: An observational upper bound constrains this conditional relation; a null tensor detection does not rule out all inflation.

before.name: Oscillating-inflaton preheating rescaled boson-mode equation
before.plain: X_k'' + omega_k² X_k=0; X_k=a^(3/2) chi_k; omega_k²=k²/a² +g² Phi² sin²(mt)+Delta
before.description: Rescaled scalar daughter-field mode equation for a massive sinusoidally oscillating inflaton coupled quadratically to a second scalar in an expanding universe.
assumptions: Two real scalar fields in a spatially flat FLRW background: homogeneous oscillating inflaton phi(t) approximately Phi(t) sin(mt) and spectator daughter field chi with interaction -g² phi² chi²/2.
The daughter Fourier mode chi_k experiences cosmological expansion a(t); X_k=a^(3/2) chi_k eliminates its leading 3H time-friction term.
The effective potential is quadratic m²phi²/2 near the inflaton minimum; the inflaton mass m and amplitude Phi(t) define oscillations.
Delta is the residual mass/expansion/curvature term m_chi²-(3/4)(dot a/a)²-(3/2)(ddot a/a)-xi R as defined in the source; the formula does not assume Delta=0 universally.
Linear initial-stage daughter-field mode treatment: nonlinear backreaction, daughter scattering, rescattering and thermalization are not represented by the displayed oscillator equation.
A static Mathieu equation with fixed resonance parameter is not generally valid for expanding-universe broad resonance; the source explicitly distinguishes stochastic-resonance regimes.
variables: X_k=a^(3/2)chi_k: friction-rescaled daughter scalar Fourier mode
before.regime: Linearized daughter-scalar-mode production for a massive near-sinusoidally oscillating homogeneous inflaton in FLRW spacetime, with specified quadratic interaction; not a complete account of nonlinear reheating, backreaction or thermalization.
before.units: Natural units c=hbar=1; k/a, m, g Phi, sqrt(|Delta|) dimension mass; omega_k² and Delta dimension mass²; t inverse mass.
before.theoryRelationship: Original source-specific linear mode amplification equation with expansion; do not equate with universal reheating dynamics or non-expanding static Mathieu-resonance bands.

sourceLocations.locator: Kofman, Linde and Starobinsky, arXiv:hep-ph/9704452v2, Sec. IV, Eq. (38) and Eq. (39), printed p. 12 (PDF page 12); Delta definition immediately under (39). Sec. V, printed pp. 12–13 discusses expanding-universe stochastic resonance beyond a static Mathieu approximation.

after.name: SIDM local mean-free-path cross section
after.description: Elastic self-scattering cross section corresponding to the original proposal's fixed local dark-matter density.
assumptions: Uses the source's local mass density 0.4 GeV/cm^3 and the dilute-particle mean-free-path relation lambda=1/(n_x sigma_XX).
Cold, nondissipative, elastic same-species scattering; negligible annihilation in the original example.
The coefficient and quoted mean-free-path interval are historical illustrative assumptions, not current observational bounds or a universal preferred SIDM cross section.
For velocity-dependent or anisotropic scattering, distinguish total, transfer and viscosity cross sections; do not substitute them silently.
variables: sigma_XX: total elastic self-scattering cross section in cm^2
m_x: particle rest mass expressed in GeV with c=1
lambda: local mean free path expressed in Mpc
after.regime: Dilute local halo under the fixed density convention; not a full halo-evolution model.
after.units: Cross section has area units; displayed mass and length ratios are dimensionless.
after.theoryRelationship: Elastic self-scattering cross section corresponding to the original proposal's fixed local dark-matter density. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Spergel & Steinhardt, Eq. (1), printed p. 2, paragraph beginning “To be more specific”. arXiv:astro-ph/9909386v2, PDF page 2.

after.name: Original two-field hybrid-inflation potential
after.description: Linde's specific two-field potential whose waterfall instability occurs when the sigma-direction mass squared changes sign.
assumptions: Canonical scalar-field example in Einstein gravity; lambda>0, g^2>0, positive mass scales M and m.
Along sigma=0, m_sigma^2=g^2 phi^2-M^2; the stable inflationary valley requires |phi|>M/g, and loss of stability triggers a possible waterfall.
Inflation and rapid completion require suitable initial conditions and parameter hierarchies; the potential alone does not establish sufficient e-folds or observational agreement.
The original text interprets sigma as a nonnegative Higgs radial degree of freedom to avoid treating its two signs as separate physical vacua.
after.regime: Original canonical two-field hybrid-inflation example, not every hybrid or supersymmetric variant.
after.units: c=hbar=1; fields and M,m have mass dimension 1, V dimension 4.
after.theoryRelationship: Linde's specific two-field potential whose waterfall instability occurs when the sigma-direction mass squared changes sign. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Linde, Hybrid Inflation, Sec. 2, Eq. (1), printed p. 3 and the immediately following waterfall discussion. arXiv:astro-ph/9307002v3, PDF page 3.

after.name: Warm-inflation overdamped mean-field drift
after.description: Thermally averaged overdamped inflaton drift after neglecting acceleration and small fluctuations in Berera's warm-inflation example.
assumptions: Source Eq. (2) first places the expression inside a thermal average; the next paragraph removes brackets when the mean field is much larger than its fluctuations and defines Gamma_phi as the averaged dissipation coefficient.
Requires potential dominance phi_dot^2/2 much less than V and negligible acceleration compared with (3H+Gamma_phi)phi_dot, source Eqs. (4)-(5).
Homogeneous coarse-grained mean field in a thermal bath, Gamma_phi>=0; omits stochastic noise and does not assert that a Markovian local coefficient exists for every microscopic model.
Do not mistake this slow-roll equation for the full second-order equation or an independently complete radiation/temperature evolution system.
variables: phi: homogeneous thermally averaged scalar field
V_,phi: derivative of the finite-temperature effective potential with respect to phi
after.regime: Thermal mean-field slow roll in the illustrative warm-inflation regime.
after.units: c=hbar=k_B=1; H and Gamma_phi have mass dimension 1, phi dimension 1, all equation terms dimension 3.
after.theoryRelationship: Thermally averaged overdamped inflaton drift after neglecting acceleration and small fluctuations in Berera's warm-inflation example. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Berera, Warm Inflation, Eq. (2) and following averaging paragraph; validity conditions Eqs. (4)-(5), printed p. 3. arXiv:astro-ph/9509049v1, PDF page 3.

after.name: Wrong-sign scalar phantom stress-energy
after.description: Homogeneous energy density and pressure of Caldwell's wrong-sign scalar toy model.
assumptions: Metric signature (+---) and scalar Lagrangian L_phi=-g^{mu nu}partial_mu phi partial_nu phi/2-V, exactly the source convention.
Homogeneous minimally coupled scalar in an expanding cosmological background; no spatial-gradient contribution in this display.
Positive energy requires V>phi_dot^2/2; for nonzero phi_dot this gives w=p/rho<-1, while phi_dot=0 gives w=-1.
Wrong-sign kinetic energy is a ghost at the quantum level; this phenomenological toy model is not claimed to be a stable ultraviolet-complete dark-energy theory.
after.regime: Classical homogeneous phantom toy model, not a stability result or evidence for w<-1.
after.units: c=hbar=1; field dimension 1, dot(phi) dimension 2, rho,p,V dimension 4.
after.theoryRelationship: Homogeneous energy density and pressure of Caldwell's wrong-sign scalar toy model. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Caldwell, A Phantom Menace?, unnumbered equations in paragraph beginning “We describe the system of gravitation”, PDF p. 4. arXiv:astro-ph/9908168v2, PDF page 4.

after.name: TeVeS physical-to-Einstein metric relation
after.description: Disformal relation defining the matter-coupled physical metric in Bekenstein's original TeVeS construction.
assumptions: Einstein metric g has signature (-+++); the timelike vector obeys g^{alpha beta}U_alpha U_beta=-1.
U_alpha is lowered with g, not with the physical metric; phi is dimensionless.
Matter minimally couples to g_tilde; gravitational scalar/vector/tensor dynamics require the separate action and field equations.
This structural definition does not establish cosmological viability, stability or agreement with later multimessenger constraints.
variables: U_alpha: covariant unit timelike vector with normalization defined using g
after.regime: Original tensor-vector-scalar gravitational model.
after.units: Dimensionless metric components in coordinates of common length units; phi and unit-vector components are dimensionless under this convention.
after.theoryRelationship: Disformal relation defining the matter-coupled physical metric in Bekenstein's original TeVeS construction. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Bekenstein, Sec. III, Eq. (22), printed p. 9; vector normalization Eq. (20) on PDF p. 8. arXiv:astro-ph/0403694v6, PDF page 9.

after.name: Sterile-neutrino vacuum seesaw mixing limit
after.plain: theta_vac approx mu/M for mu much less than M
after.description: Small vacuum active-sterile mixing in the one-generation mass model used by Dodelson and Widrow.
assumptions: One active and one sterile neutrino, Dirac mixing mass mu and right-handed Majorana mass M; no active Majorana mass in the source setup.
Leading order in mu/M; theta_vac labels the source's theta_M specifically evaluated in vacuum, not the finite-temperature mixing angle.
This does not supply a relic abundance, production kernel, resonant conversion result, or current viability bound for sterile-neutrino dark matter.
Do not use the paper's historical cosmological normalization or keV mass preferences as current constraints.
after.regime: Vacuum one-generation seesaw hierarchy; not in-medium oscillation kinetics.
after.units: mu and M share mass units; theta is dimensionless (radians).
after.theoryRelationship: Small vacuum active-sterile mixing in the one-generation mass model used by Dodelson and Widrow. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Dodelson & Widrow, immediately after Eq. (1), paragraph beginning “In vacuum”, printed p. 4. Source writes theta_M=mu/M in the stated limit. arXiv:hep-ph/9303287v1, PDF page 4.

after.name: Primordial-black-hole near-critical mass scaling
after.description: Near-threshold collapse scaling applied to the primordial-black-hole initial mass function.
assumptions: Applies only near the black-hole-formation threshold for a fixed family of initial perturbation profiles and equation of state.
delta is the source's dimensionless control parameter/density contrast; its slicing, smoothing and profile convention must accompany numerical threshold values.
K carries mass units and depends on the profile and horizon scale; it is not a universal dimensionless constant.
The radiation-fluid critical exponent is approximately 0.356 in the cited calculation, not a universal exponent for every matter model.
This is a formation scaling law, not a claim that PBHs supply all dark matter, nor a present-day abundance/constraint calculation.
variables: K: positive mass normalization for the chosen perturbation family
after.regime: Classical near-critical radiation-fluid collapse; not evaporation or arbitrary far-supercritical overdensities.
after.units: M_BH and K have mass units; delta, delta_c and gamma are dimensionless.
after.theoryRelationship: Near-threshold collapse scaling applied to the primordial-black-hole initial mass function. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Niemeyer & Jedamzik, Eq. (1), PDF p. 1; radiation-fluid application and gamma approximately 0.356 discussed on PDF p. 2. arXiv:astro-ph/9709072v2, PDF page 1.

after.name: Dark-photon induced electromagnetic-current coupling
after.plain: L_int contains epsilon e A_prime_mu J_EM^mu; epsilon=epsilon_Y cos(theta_W)
after.description: Low-energy electromagnetic-current coupling induced by hypercharge kinetic mixing for a massive dark photon.
assumptions: Uses the authors' field-redefinition and sign convention A_mu -> A_mu+epsilon A_prime_mu; flipping A_prime changes the displayed coupling sign without changing observables.
Small kinetic mixing, massive extra U(1) gauge boson, and low energies where Z-mixing effects are suppressed.
J_EM is normalized so the ordinary photon interaction is e A_mu J_EM^mu; electric charge is not included twice in J_EM.
This coupling alone does not specify a dark-matter abundance or require the vector itself to constitute dark matter; massless limits and hidden-sector millicharges need separate treatment.
variables: J_EM^mu: electromagnetic current with charges in units of e
after.regime: Low-energy massive-dark-photon portal in the perturbatively small-mixing approximation.
after.units: c=hbar=1; e and epsilon dimensionless, vector dimension 1, current dimension 3, L_int dimension 4.
after.theoryRelationship: Low-energy electromagnetic-current coupling induced by hypercharge kinetic mixing for a massive dark photon. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Bjorken, Essig, Schuster & Toro, Sec. II.A, paragraph immediately after Eq. (3), PDF p. 3, unnumbered field-redefinition-induced current coupling. arXiv:0906.0580v1, PDF page 3.

after.name: Affleck–Dine inflationary flat-direction potential
after.plain: V=-c H_I^2 |phi|^2+[a lambda H_I phi^n/(n M^(n-3))+h.c.]+|lambda|^2 |phi|^(2n-2)/M^(2n-6)
after.description: Inflationary potential for a supersymmetric Affleck–Dine flat direction with a negative Hubble-induced mass and a nonrenormalizable lifting operator.
assumptions: The specific negative-mass scenario of Dine–Randall–Thomas Sec. 4.1: c>0 and H_I nearly constant during inflation.
H_I much greater than gravitino mass, so low-energy hidden-sector soft terms are neglected here.
Complex flat-direction scalar phi, n>3 integer, cutoff M, dimensionless coupling lambda and complex Hubble-induced A-term coefficient a.
The phase-sensitive A term is one ingredient of charge generation; later evolution, decay/reheating and washout are needed for a baryon-to-entropy prediction.
Potential is an effective description below its cutoff and not applicable to every Affleck–Dine realization.
variables: phi: complex flat-direction field, mass dimension 1
h.c.: Hermitian conjugate of the preceding term
after.regime: High-Hubble-scale inflationary flat-direction example, before low-energy soft terms become important.
after.units: c=hbar=1; each term has mass dimension 4; n>3.
after.theoryRelationship: Inflationary potential for a supersymmetric Affleck–Dine flat direction with a negative Hubble-induced mass and a nonrenormalizable lifting operator. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Dine, Randall & Thomas, Sec. 4.1 “The Inflationary Epoch”, Eq. (18), printed p. 20 (PDF p. 21). arXiv:hep-ph/9507453v1, PDF page 21.

after.name: Asymmetric-dark-matter density scaling
after.plain: Omega_DM approximately of order (m_DM/m_B) Omega_B when n_DM is of order n_B
after.description: Order-of-magnitude density scaling when dark and baryon asymmetries have comparable number densities.
assumptions: Nonrelativistic relics with efficient depletion of the symmetric particle-antiparticle component.
A model-dependent transfer mechanism relates surviving dark and baryon asymmetries; n_DM~n_B is an assumption, not an exact conservation law.
The displayed relation is approximate: charge assignments, chemical equilibrium, decoupling, sphalerons and residual symmetric populations change the ratio.
Does not impose a universal 5 GeV dark-matter mass or repeat the historical paper's observational density values as current measurements.
variables: Omega_DM,Omega_B: present dark-matter and baryon density fractions relative to the same critical density
after.regime: Asymmetry-dominated nonrelativistic relic populations with comparable number asymmetries.
after.units: Density fractions and mass ratio dimensionless.
after.theoryRelationship: Order-of-magnitude density scaling when dark and baryon asymmetries have comparable number densities. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Kaplan, Luty & Zurek, Introduction, final paragraph of printed p. 1 (PDF p. 2), unnumbered n_DM and Omega_DM scaling; annihilation condition summarized on next page. arXiv:0901.4117v1, PDF page 2.

after.name: Cosmic-string VOS correlation-length evolution
after.description: Phenomenological long-string correlation-length evolution in the velocity-dependent one-scale model.
assumptions: Averaged long-string network in spatially flat FRW, with rho_inf=mu/L^2.
v_inf is energy-weighted RMS string speed, not a single segment velocity; units c=1.
ell_f is the background-friction damping length; c_tilde is a calibrated loop-chopping efficiency.
This length equation must be paired with the velocity equation and a momentum-parameter prescription for predictive evolution.
This version omits the later-added radiation-backreaction term and does not automatically cover currents, multiple tensions, junctions or a detailed loop distribution.
variables: mu: string energy per unit length
after.regime: Coarse-grained long-string network model, not microscopic field equations or a direct detection claim.
after.units: c=1; time and length have identical units; every displayed term is a speed/dimensionless.
after.theoryRelationship: Phenomenological long-string correlation-length evolution in the velocity-dependent one-scale model. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Martins & Shellard, Sec. II.A, Eq. (2.3), printed/PDF p. 2; rho_inf definition and loop-loss convention precede it. arXiv:hep-ph/0003298v1, PDF page 2.

after.name: Canonical curvature mode during matter-like contraction
after.description: Canonical scalar curvature-mode equation specialized to the matter-like contracting background of Finelli and Brandenberger.
assumptions: Explicit specialization of source Eq. (14) at p=2/3, giving p(2p-1)/(p-1)^2=2.
Spatially flat Einstein gravity with one canonical scalar and the exponential-potential power-law background; negative cosmic time approaches the putative bounce at t=0.
v=z zeta with z=a phi_dot/H; primes are conformal-time derivatives and k is comoving wavenumber.
Matter-like means the scalar background has w=0; this is not the perturbation equation of a pressureless fluid with sound speed zero.

Sub-Hubble vacuum initial conditions plus this background give scale-invariant growing pre-bounce curvature modes; transfer through a stable nonsingular bounce, anisotropy control and phenomenological viability remain separate unresolved model choices.
variables: v_k: Fourier mode of canonically normalized scalar perturbation
t: cosmic time, t<0 on contracting branch
after.regime: Linear adiabatic modes before the bounce in a canonical scalar w=0 contracting solution.
after.units: c=hbar=1; a dimensionless, eta has length dimension, k inverse length; v double-prime and k^2 v have matching dimensions regardless of Fourier normalization.
after.theoryRelationship: Canonical scalar curvature-mode equation specialized to the matter-like contracting background of Finelli and Brandenberger. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Finelli & Brandenberger, Sec. II, Eq. (14) specialized at p=2/3; definitions Eqs. (7)-(8),(13), PDF p. 3 and explicit p=2/3 discussion on p. 4. arXiv:hep-th/0112249v2, PDF page 3.

after.name: Group-field condensate mean-field equation
after.plain: integral d^4g_prime K(g_I,g_I_prime) sigma(g_I_prime) + lambda [functional derivative of V with respect to conjugate_varphi(g_I), evaluated at varphi=sigma] = 0
after.description: Nonlinear group-field-theory condensate equation for the specific single-particle coherent-state ansatz.
assumptions: Source action has quadratic kernel K plus interaction lambda V; sigma is the coherent condensate wavefunction, not a spacetime scalar inflaton.
This record follows the source's Riemannian four-argument SO(4) construction with simplicity/gauge restrictions, not an arbitrary Lorentzian noncompact-group generalization.
I labels four group arguments and d^4g is product Haar measure, not integration over four-dimensional spacetime.
Uses the single-particle coherent condensate Eq. (13) and its gauge/homogeneity invariances; this is a mean-field truncation with neglected higher correlations.
A choice of GFT kernel, interactions, quantum state and reconstruction is necessary before obtaining a cosmological Friedmann equation.
Does not assert the emergent semiclassical limit, observational validity or universality of a bounce across all GFT models.
variables: K: chosen quadratic GFT kinetic kernel
varphi,bar_varphi: complex GFT field and conjugate
V: GFT interaction functional, not a local scalar potential
d^4g_prime: product of four invariant group measures
after.regime: Coherent mean-field group-field cosmology ansatz; not the exact full many-body quantum dynamics.
after.units: Group coordinates and normalized Haar measures are dimensionless; K, lambda and V inherit the chosen GFT action normalization. Both terms have identical field-equation units; there is no model-independent SI length/time assignment for sigma.
after.theoryRelationship: Nonlinear group-field-theory condensate equation for the specific single-particle coherent-state ansatz. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Gielen, Oriti & Sindoni, “Effective cosmological dynamics”, Eq. (18), PDF p. 3; action Eq. (16), coherent-state ansatz Eq. (13). arXiv:1303.3576v3, PDF page 3.

after.name: Euclidean dipole spinfoam cosmology amplitude
after.plain: W(z_i,z_f) approx N^2 z_i z_f exp[-(z_i^2+z_f^2)/(2 t hbar)]
after.description: Approximate homogeneous-isotropic transition amplitude in the Euclidean dipole, single-vertex, large-volume construction.
assumptions: Three essential truncations: fixed dipole graph, first single-vertex term of the spinfoam expansion, and large volume.
Uses Euclidean rather than physical Lorentzian spinfoam dynamics, no matter sector, and the paper's coherent-boundary normalization.
z=alpha c+i beta p labels intrinsic/extrinsic geometry; t is heat-kernel width parameter, NOT cosmic time.
Both boundary labels appear holomorphically because of the source boundary-orientation convention; reversing the final orientation changes z_f to -conjugate(z_f).
The leading amplitude factorizes and should not be promoted to a generic connected transition amplitude, a complete quantum cosmology or a proven bounce.
variables: z_i,z_f: complex homogeneous-isotropic coherent boundary labels
alpha,beta: constants mapping c,p to dimensionless boundary labels
after.regime: Euclidean, matter-free, fixed-graph, leading-vertex, large-volume approximation.
after.units: z is dimensionless and t hbar is dimensionless in the heat-kernel convention; N depends on normalization. W is an amplitude, not a probability.
after.theoryRelationship: Approximate homogeneous-isotropic transition amplitude in the Euclidean dipole, single-vertex, large-volume construction. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Bianchi, Rovelli & Vidotto, Eq. (37), PDF p. 5; z mapping Eq. (20), boundary orientation footnote 4, and explicit truncation/Euclidean caveats Sec. V PDF p. 6. arXiv:1003.3483v1, PDF page 5.

after.name: Multifield ekpyrotic scaling solution
after.plain: a proportional to (-t)^p; p=sum_i 2/c_i^2; V=-sum_i V_i exp(-c_i phi_i)
after.description: Assisted contracting scaling solution for canonical fields with negative exponential potentials.
assumptions: Spatially flat four-dimensional Einstein gravity, canonical scalars, V_i>0 and reduced Planck units 8 pi G=1.
Contracting branch t<0; the ekpyrotic regime requires 0<p<1/3, corresponding to w>1 for the scaling background.
All participating fields follow the specific joint scaling trajectory; arbitrary initial conditions need not realize it.
The multifield trajectory is a saddle with an unstable entropy direction, not a stable attractor.
Nearly scale-invariant entropy perturbations require steep potentials and conversion to curvature perturbations; neither conversion nor a nonsingular bounce is fixed by this relation.
variables: t: cosmic time approaching zero from below
phi_i: canonical scalar fields in reduced Planck units
after.regime: Multifield negative-exponential scaling solution during ekpyrotic contraction.
after.units: 8 pi G=c=hbar=1; phi_i is measured in reduced Planck units, c_i and p dimensionless; V_i are energy-density amplitudes. Restoring units replaces c_i phi_i by c_i phi_i/M_Pl.
after.theoryRelationship: Assisted contracting scaling solution for canonical fields with negative exponential potentials. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Koyama & Wands, Sec. 2, Eq. (2) PDF p. 2 and Eq. (3) PDF p. 3; instability discussed in abstract and phase-space analysis. arXiv:hep-th/0703040v2, PDF page 3.

after.name: Cyclic-model cutoff exponential potential
after.description: Illustrative scalar potential combining a positive plateau with a negative region and a suppressed far-negative-field tail in the original cyclic proposal.
assumptions: Source uses reduced Planck units 8 pi G=1 from Eq. (6) onward.
V0>0; c is a positive slope parameter and F is chosen so that the full V tends to zero as phi tends to minus infinity.
F is nearly unity to the right of the potential minimum; its far-negative tail must suppress the exponential, not merely tend to zero at an unspecified slow rate.
The source's historical c and dark-energy density choices are illustrative, not current fits.
This potential does not by itself produce a complete cycle: matter coupling, crunch/bang matching and stable nonsingular completion are independent assumptions.
variables: phi: scalar measured in reduced Planck units
after.regime: Four-dimensional illustrative cyclic scalar effective potential, not a completed singularity-resolution mechanism.
after.units: 8 pi G=c_light=hbar=1; c phi dimensionless and V0,V have energy-density units on restoration of Planck scales.
after.theoryRelationship: Illustrative scalar potential combining a positive plateau with a negative region and a suppressed far-negative-field tail in the original cyclic proposal. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

after.name: Compact string-gas near-Hagedorn heat capacity
after.description: Near-Hagedorn closed-string heat-capacity scaling used in the thermal-fluctuation string-gas scenario.
assumptions: Gas of weakly coupled closed strings, three large toroidal dimensions and six small compact dimensions; all dimensions compact for the cited positive-heat-capacity result.
Temperature approaches the Hagedorn temperature from below; thermal equilibrium and the finite-volume string-thermodynamic regime are assumed.
R is the size scale of the large compact region; alpha_prime=l_s^2.
This is an approximate thermodynamic relation, not a generic point-particle heat capacity.

Converting thermal fluctuations to observable curvature spectra requires additional dilaton/background and perturbation-transfer assumptions which the source explicitly discusses; this relation alone does not establish a viable cosmology.
variables: C_V: heat capacity at fixed volume
R: length scale of the large compact region
alpha_prime: inverse string tension parameter, equal to l_s^2
after.regime: Weak-coupling compact closed-string thermodynamics near the Hagedorn regime.
after.units: c=hbar=k_B=1; R and l_s have length units, T inverse length, so C_V is dimensionless.
after.theoryRelationship: Near-Hagedorn closed-string heat-capacity scaling used in the thermal-fluctuation string-gas scenario. This is one model-level relation, not completion or empirical confirmation of the theory family.

sourceLocations.locator: Nayeri, Brandenberger & Vafa, “Computation of the Spectrum”, Eq. (9), PDF p. 3; compactness assumptions and gravitational-transfer caveats on pp. 3-4. arXiv:hep-th/0511140v2, PDF page 3.

after.name: Formal free third-quantized superspace action
after.plain: S2 = -1/2 integral D(3g) Phi[3g] Box_sup Phi[3g]
after.description: Formal quadratic superspace-field action in the Giddings–Strominger third-quantization proposal.
assumptions: Follows the original formal Euclidean sum-over-four-geometries interpretation with fixed spatial topology S^3 at a boundary and an implicit ultraviolet cutoff.

Phi is a field on the configuration space of spatial geometries, not an ordinary spacetime matter field; Box_sup labels the source's Wheeler–DeWitt superspace operator, not the spacetime d’Alembertian.

The authors explicitly state that Eq. (4.1) is incomplete: its equation of motion implements only an integrated constraint, not all local gravitational constraints. Their BRST/ghost extension begins in Eq. (4.2).
This is the free quadratic term only. Topology-changing interactions, measure/gauge choices and quantum corrections are additional ingredients, not supplied by this display.

The formal functional integral is not established as a mathematically well-defined complete quantum-gravity theory; no observed baby universes or solution of the cosmological-constant problem is inferred.
variables: 3g: spatial three-metric, serving as a superspace coordinate
D(3g): formal functional measure over spatial geometries with gauge treatment required
Phi[3g]: real superspace field creating/annihilating single-universe states in the proposed interpretation
after.regime: Formal free superspace-field construction before full constraint/BRST and interacting completion.
after.units: Natural action convention hbar=1. Functional measure, field and operator normalizations are formal; their combined normalization makes S2 dimensionless. No universal local spacetime engineering dimension for Phi is asserted.
after.theoryRelationship: Source-specific historical free-action proposal, explicitly schematic and constraint-incomplete; not model-family completion or an empirically verified multiverse mechanism.

sourceLocations.locator: Giddings & Strominger, HUTP-88/A036 (June 1988 preprint of 1989 paper), Sec. 4, Eq. (4.1), printed p. 12, KEK scan PDF p. 6 right-hand page. Constraint-incompleteness warning and BRST extension Eq. (4.2) are printed p. 13, PDF p. 8 left-hand page. Scan page order is not monotonic.

after.name: EFT inflation scalar sound speed
after.description: Scalar propagation speed in the leading two-derivative Goldstone action.
assumptions: Single clock; spatially flat FLRW background.
Decoupling regime with slowly varying coefficients; omit higher-spatial-derivative dispersion.
Hdot < 0 and a positive time-kinetic coefficient; predictions require energies below the EFT cutoff.
variables: c_s: dimensionless scalar speed relative to light
M_2^4: coefficient of (delta g^00)^2/2, not a particle mass measurement
Hdot: cosmic-time derivative of the Hubble rate
after.regime: Leading quadratic Goldstone sector, not every multifield or higher-derivative model.
after.units: c = hbar = 1; M_2^4 and M_Pl^2 Hdot both have mass dimension four.
after.theoryRelationship: Ratio of gradient and time-kinetic coefficients; not an observed sound-speed value.

sourceLocations.locator: Cheung et al., arXiv:0709.0293v2, Section 4.2, Eqs. (37)–(38), printed p. 12 (PDF p. 12); decoupling restrictions in Section 3.

after.name: Representative axion-like early-dark-energy potential
after.plain: V(phi) = V0 [1 - cos(phi/f)]^n; averaged w_phi approximately (n - 1)/(n + 1)
after.description: Representative potential and late oscillation average, not a universal EDE law.
assumptions: Canonical homogeneous scalar; V0 > 0 and n > 0.
The equation-of-state average requires rapid small-amplitude oscillations near a minimum, where V is proportional to phi^(2n).
The average is invalid during freezing, onset of rolling or anharmonic large-amplitude evolution.
n = 2 gives radiation-like dilution; n > 2 dilutes faster. Perturbations require separate evolution.
variables: w_phi: scalar pressure divided by scalar energy density, averaged over oscillations
after.regime: Oscillating scalar subtype; no statement about generic tracking EDE or late-time quintessence.
after.units: c = hbar = 1; phi and f have mass dimension one, V0 has dimension four, w is dimensionless.
after.theoryRelationship: Potential specified up to normalization in Poulin et al.; the averaged w describes an asymptotic regime, not proof of fit to all cosmological data.

after.scientificStatus: Successful model-building framework; the mechanism and microscopic inflaton remain unconfirmed.
after.coreIdea: A period of accelerated expansion shrinks the comoving Hubble radius and can prepare the conditions for the hot Big Bang.
after.degreesOfFreedom: Background geometry and model-dependent matter; the displayed representative is one canonical scalar.
assumptions: For the displayed slow-roll parameters: minimal coupling, one canonical field, smooth positive potential and potential-dominated evolution.
Inflation means accelerated expansion; potential slow roll is a useful sufficient regime, not its definition.
The hot-Big-Bang connection requires an end to acceleration and subsequent energy transfer; accelerated expansion alone does not specify reheating.
after.mathematicalStructure: Einstein–scalar dynamics; epsilon_H = -Hdot/H² < 1 during inflation. Potential epsilon_V and eta_V approximate the background only under slow roll.
after.regime: Semiclassical expanding cosmology below a specified effective-theory cutoff.
predictionsConsequences: Enough expansion suppresses spatial curvature; observable predictions require a perturbation mechanism and an exit into reheating.
The canonical slow-roll regime ties the potential slope and curvature to the evolution that controls primordial spectra.
after.evidenceSummary: CMB scalar spectra and tensor limits constrain specified inflationary models, not inflation independently of their perturbation and post-inflation histories.
after.whatEvidenceDoesNotEstablish: Neither a unique potential nor an initial-state prescription or ultraviolet completion is identified.
limitations: The number of observable e-folds depends on reheating.
Slow-roll expressions fail outside their assumptions.
usefulDiscriminators: Compare tilt, tensors and non-Gaussianity at the same pivot and with matched reheating assumptions.
unresolvedQuestions: What drives accelerated expansion and ends it?

after.regime: Early-universe curvature regime of the specified effective gravity model.

The range -1 ≤ w ≤ 1 requires positive energy density and nonnegative potential.

limitations: Canonical positive-energy fields do not cross below w = -1.
Background degeneracies and potential tuning remain.
usefulDiscriminators: Test expansion and growth together, checking whether the inferred history stays inside the canonical-field domain.
unresolvedQuestions: Which potential and initial conditions produce viable late acceleration?

after.coreIdea: Modes entering the long-wavelength sector induce stochastic forcing in its effective dynamics.
after.degreesOfFreedom: A coarse-grained inflaton and its probability distribution, after separating short and long wavelengths.
assumptions: Displayed equations use one canonical field at leading slow-roll order and e-fold time N = ln a.
Gaussian white noise has zero mean and delta correlation in N; the Fokker–Planck equation uses the Itô prescription.
Specify initial data and boundary conditions for the probability distribution; the displayed equation does not by itself select absorbing boundaries or volume weighting.
after.mathematicalStructure: A Langevin equation and its Fokker–Planck counterpart describe drift and diffusion.
after.regime: Long-wavelength effective dynamics; validity depends on coarse graining and the slow-roll/noise approximation.

The corresponding Fokker–Planck equation tracks probability flow from classical drift and quantum-induced diffusion.

after.whatEvidenceDoesNotEstablish: The equations alone do not establish eternal inflation, a multiverse measure or a fundamental collapse law.

A volume-weighted distribution is not automatically a normalized probability.

after.coreIdea: Inflationary energy is transferred into particles; resonant preheating and later equilibration are distinct stages.
after.degreesOfFreedom: An inflaton condensate, produced field modes and subsequently interacting particle distributions.
assumptions: Displayed mode equation assumes a quadratic inflaton potential and a two-scalar interaction proportional to phi² chi².

The full frequency includes expansion and any retained mass or curvature terms; neglecting them requires a separate comparison of scales.

after.regime: Initial particle production before nonlinear backreaction and rescattering dominate.

before.name: Dark matter
before.shortQuestion: What physical component or modification of gravitational dynamics accounts for the nonluminous gravitating matter inferred across galaxies, clusters, the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure?
before.whyItMatters: A cold nonbaryonic dark component is central to the standard cosmological model, but its microscopic identity has not been established. Candidate particles and fields span enormous parameter ranges, compact-object scenarios are constrained but not eliminated in every mass window, and modified-gravity approaches address parts of the phenomenology with different assumptions.
establishedBackground: The ΛCDM framework successfully describes a wide range of cosmological observations using a cold dark-matter component, but this does not identify the underlying particle or field.
Direct, indirect and collider searches constrain candidate interactions and masses rather than testing one unique dark-matter theory.
Axions, WIMPs, ultralight fields, sterile neutrinos, self-interacting dark matter and primordial black holes represent physically distinct candidate classes.
Modified-gravity frameworks such as MOND address selected astrophysical regularities but must also confront cluster, lensing and cosmological observations.

approachGroups.name: Cosmological baseline
approachGroups.description: Treats cold dark matter as a gravitating component in the standard cosmological model without specifying its microphysics.

approachGroups.name: Particle and field candidates
approachGroups.description: Introduces new particles, fields or production mechanisms with testable parameter spaces.

approachGroups.name: Compact-object candidates
approachGroups.description: Uses primordial black holes or related compact populations over allowed mass fractions/windows.

approachGroups.name: Modified-gravity alternatives
approachGroups.description: Changes gravitational dynamics instead of, or in addition to, introducing a new dark component.

keyAssumptions: The cosmological model used to infer the dark component and its primordial abundance.
The local halo model, nuclear response and detector assumptions used in direct-search constraints.
The production mechanism and interaction structure for a particle or field candidate.
Whether an alternative-gravity model can fit cosmological as well as galactic/cluster-scale data.
before.developmentContext: DESI events constrain the background cosmological model and dark-energy sector; they are not direct detections of dark matter. LZ is a direct-search development and its 2026 excess remains a 2.6σ global candidate signal rather than a discovery.
before.currentStatus: The gravitational evidence motivating dark matter is extensive, while the microscopic nature of the dark component remains unidentified. Current experimental and observational results constrain candidate models and parameter space rather than selecting one established microphysical explanation.
openIssues: Identify or exclude viable particle/field candidates across poorly constrained mass and coupling regimes.
Reconcile small-scale structure phenomenology with particle physics and baryonic astrophysics.
Discriminate a dark component from modified-gravity explanations across galactic, cluster and cosmological scales.

after.whyItMatters: A cold nonbaryonic dark component is central to the standard cosmological model, but its microscopic identity has not been established. Candidate particles and fields span enormous parameter ranges, compact-object scenarios are constrained but not eliminated in every mass window, and modified-gravity approaches address parts of the phenomenology with different assumptions.
establishedBackground: The ΛCDM framework successfully describes a wide range of cosmological observations using a cold dark-matter component, but this does not identify the underlying particle or field.
Direct, indirect and collider searches constrain candidate interactions and masses rather than testing one unique dark-matter theory.
Axions, WIMPs, ultralight fields, sterile neutrinos, self-interacting dark matter and primordial black holes represent physically distinct candidate classes.
Modified-gravity frameworks such as MOND address selected astrophysical regularities but must also confront cluster, lensing and cosmological observations.

approachGroups.name: Cosmological baseline
approachGroups.description: Treats cold dark matter as a gravitating component in the standard cosmological model without specifying its microphysics.

approachGroups.name: Particle and field candidates
approachGroups.description: Introduces new particles, fields or production mechanisms with testable parameter spaces.

approachGroups.name: Compact-object candidates
approachGroups.description: Uses primordial black holes or related compact populations over allowed mass fractions/windows.

approachGroups.name: Modified-gravity alternatives
approachGroups.description: Changes gravitational dynamics instead of, or in addition to, introducing a new dark component.

keyAssumptions: The cosmological model used to infer the dark component and its primordial abundance.
The local halo model, nuclear response and detector assumptions used in direct-search constraints.
The production mechanism and interaction structure for a particle or field candidate.
Whether an alternative-gravity model can fit cosmological as well as galactic/cluster-scale data.
after.developmentContext: DESI events constrain the background cosmological model and dark-energy sector; they are not direct detections of dark matter. LZ is a direct-search development and its 2026 excess remains a 2.6σ global candidate signal rather than a discovery.
after.currentStatus: The gravitational evidence motivating dark matter is extensive, while the microscopic nature of the dark component remains unidentified. Current experimental and observational results constrain candidate models and parameter space rather than selecting one established microphysical explanation.
openIssues: Identify or exclude viable particle/field candidates across poorly constrained mass and coupling regimes.
Reconcile small-scale structure phenomenology with particle physics and baryonic astrophysics.
Discriminate a dark component from modified-gravity explanations across galactic, cluster and cosmological scales.

after.name: Inflationary mechanism and initial conditions
after.shortQuestion: What dynamics, initial state and exit history generated the primordial perturbations?
after.whyItMatters: Different inflationary dynamics can produce similar scalar spectra, so reconstructing the early Universe requires connecting observations to initial conditions, fluctuation dynamics and reheating.
establishedBackground: CMB measurements constrain perturbation statistics; they do not identify an inflaton.
The BK18 tensor result is an upper limit, not a rejection of every inflationary scenario.

approachGroups.name: Background dynamics
approachGroups.description: Compare potential-driven and curvature-driven inflationary backgrounds rather than treating inflation as one potential.

approachGroups.name: Primordial fluctuation predictions
approachGroups.description: Relate background dynamics to scalar and tensor statistics; matching those statistics does not identify a unique microscopic model.

approachGroups.name: Stochastic evolution and initial conditions
approachGroups.description: Study coarse-grained field evolution and its domain of validity separately from an observational reconstruction of initial conditions.

approachGroups.name: Exit and thermal-history reconstruction
approachGroups.description: Relate inflationary predictions to the subsequent reheating history rather than assuming instantaneous conversion to a thermal bath.

keyAssumptions: Likelihood, foreground and late-time cosmology affect inference.
Predictions depend on initial state and reheating history.
after.developmentContext: Evidence dates identify particular analyses, not a claim to exhaust all later measurements.
after.currentStatus: The linked CMB analyses restrict primordial spectra and tensor amplitudes, but do not establish a unique inflationary mechanism, initial quantum state or reheating history.
openIssues: Identify discriminating tensor, isocurvature or higher-correlation signals.
Test sensitivity to initial conditions and reheating rather than fitting only a spectral tilt.
Determine when the single-clock EFT and stochastic approximations remain controlled for a proposed background.

after.name: Origin of the baryon asymmetry
after.shortQuestion: Which dynamical process produced the cosmic matter–antimatter imbalance?
after.whyItMatters: Light-element and cosmic-background observations constrain the surviving baryon abundance, but identifying its dynamical origin would connect cosmology with otherwise inaccessible particle interactions.
establishedBackground: BBN connects light-element abundances to the baryon density.
Sakharov conditions organize conventional dynamical baryogenesis proposals.

approachGroups.name: Consistency conditions
approachGroups.description: Sakharov conditions organize conventional dynamical baryogenesis; they are requirements, not a calculation of the final abundance.

approachGroups.name: Scalar-condensate baryogenesis
approachGroups.description: Affleck–Dine dynamics is a distinct scalar-field route, not an alias of heavy-neutrino decay.

approachGroups.name: Lepton-asymmetry generation and conversion
approachGroups.description: Leptogenesis must connect production, washout and electroweak conversion to the surviving baryon abundance.

approachGroups.name: Neutrino-mass model interface
approachGroups.description: Seesaw models can supply particle content for leptogenesis, but neutrino masses alone do not demonstrate successful baryogenesis.

keyAssumptions: Standard thermal-history assumptions enter BBN inference.
A CP asymmetry alone is insufficient; transport and washout matter.
after.developmentContext: Evidence dates identify particular analyses, not a claim to exhaust all later measurements.
after.currentStatus: The observed baryon abundance is not a detection of leptogenesis or any particular baryogenesis model.
openIssues: Determine viable CP violation and out-of-equilibrium dynamics.
Connect the final abundance to independently testable particle parameters.
Separate evidence for neutrino mixing or mass from evidence for the CP-violating dynamics and cosmological history needed by leptogenesis.

after.name: Dark energy and expansion-history tensions
after.shortQuestion: Are expansion-history discrepancies due to systematics, model assumptions, or new cosmic dynamics?
after.whyItMatters: Determining whether expansion-history discrepancies reflect calibration, statistical or astrophysical systematics, or new dynamics is essential before interpreting a fitted equation of state as fundamental physics.
establishedBackground: BAO distances are interpreted with a sound-horizon calibration and cosmological model.
A cosmological constant and dynamical alternatives must be compared using explicit dataset combinations.

approachGroups.name: Baseline and calibration
approachGroups.description: Use Lambda-CDM as an explicit comparison model, keeping sound-horizon calibration distinct from directly measured angular or redshift separations.

approachGroups.name: Canonical late-time scalar dynamics
approachGroups.description: Quintessence provides time-dependent late-time dynamics without making every departure from a cosmological constant evidence for a particular scalar potential.

approachGroups.name: Alternative late-time dynamics
approachGroups.description: Noncanonical kinetic models and phantom phenomenology have different assumptions and stability questions; they are not interchangeable best-fit equation-of-state labels.

approachGroups.name: Early-time modifications
approachGroups.description: A transient pre-recombination component changes the sound-horizon calibration, unlike a solely late-time acceleration model.

keyAssumptions: Keep early-time H0 inference distinct from late-time distance calibration.
Dataset choices, covariances and priors can alter apparent preference.
after.developmentContext: Evidence dates identify particular analyses, not a claim to exhaust all later measurements.
after.currentStatus: No particular dynamical field or universal resolution of expansion tensions is established by these linked records.
openIssues: Test cross-dataset consistency without selecting only favorable combinations.
Distinguish early-dark-energy hypotheses from late-time equation-of-state evolution.
Check stability and perturbation evolution as well as background-distance fits when evaluating a proposed dynamical component.

after.name: Quantum-to-classical primordial perturbations
after.shortQuestion: How do quantum primordial fluctuations yield effectively classical cosmological records?
after.whyItMatters: Cosmological predictions use quantum initial fluctuations and effectively classical records; explaining that connection requires distinguishing calculable reduced-state dynamics from claims about definite outcomes.
establishedBackground: Inflationary mode evolution can produce strongly squeezed states.
Environmental decoherence can suppress accessible interference without selecting a unique interpretation.

approachGroups.name: Quantum mode evolution
approachGroups.description: Track the primordial fluctuation state and its correlation functions before replacing it by an effective classical description.

approachGroups.name: Squeezing and classical-statistical limits
approachGroups.description: Strongly squeezed states can reproduce particular classical stochastic statistics; this does not by itself select a definite-outcome interpretation.

approachGroups.name: Environmental decoherence
approachGroups.description: Trace explicitly identified environmental degrees of freedom and test suppression of interference in the chosen subsystem.

approachGroups.name: Coarse-grained stochastic dynamics
approachGroups.description: Treat stochastic inflation as a controlled effective description where justified, not an observational proof of fundamental collapse.

keyAssumptions: Specify the subsystem, environment and coarse graining.
Do not identify a classical stochastic representation with proof of fundamental collapse.
after.developmentContext: Evidence dates identify particular analyses, not a claim to exhaust all later measurements.
after.currentStatus: Squeezing/decoherence provide a theoretical route to effective classicality; the cited CMB data do not directly establish that route.
openIssues: Identify observables sensitive to genuinely quantum correlations.
Separate decoherence calculations from the broader measurement problem.
Quantify sensitivity to subsystem choice, coarse-graining scale and environment instead of assuming one universal classicalization prescription.
